entries.title: Viking Age · Scandinavian societies
entries.location: Scandinavia, North Atlantic and wider exchange routes
entries.note: An archaeological and historical period, not a single empire or ethnicity. Farming, seafaring, trade, enslavement, migration and warfare connected diverse communities; the rounded museum convention differs from 793–1066 often used in British histories.

entries.title: Sámi · continuing Indigenous histories
entries.dates: Continuing histories · no single founding date
entries.location: Sápmi · northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola Peninsula
entries.note: Diverse Indigenous communities, languages and ways of life continue across state borders. There is no defensible single founding year. Norse expansion or the creation of modern Nordic states did not end Sámi histories or rights; reindeer herding is one of several livelihoods.

entries.title: Norway · kingdoms, unions and modern state
entries.note: A broad historical frame, not uninterrupted independent sovereignty. Consolidation of medieval kingship was gradual; c. 900 rounds the late ninth-century tradition. Danish rule and union with Sweden intervened; the latter ended in 1905. The present kingdom’s borders and institutions developed over time.

entries.title: Sweden · medieval kingdom and modern state
entries.dates: Middle Ages–present · no single founding year
entries.note: Sweden emerged gradually as a unified medieval kingdom; no precise founding year is implied. The Kalmar Union and the 1523 election of Gustav Vasa were major political changes. A realm’s shifting boundaries should not be confused with the origins of its peoples.

entries.title: Denmark · kingdom and modern state
entries.note: A selected political frame anchored around Harald Bluetooth’s conversion and Jelling monument, rather than a founding date for Denmark or Danish people. The Kalmar Union, territorial losses, the 1849 constitution and German occupation in 1940–1945 belong to different political phases; the Danish Realm extends beyond European Denmark.

entries.title: Iceland · Commonwealth, unions and republic
entries.note: 930 marks the establishment of the Althing, not first human settlement. The Commonwealth came under Norway in 1262–1264 and later Danish rule; sovereignty in 1918 retained a common monarch, and the republic was established in 1944. These were different constitutional arrangements.

entries.title: Finland · independent state
entries.note: Parliament approved independence on 6 December 1917; the republic’s constitution followed in 1919. This dates the selected independent state, not Finnish or Sámi origins. Earlier Swedish rule and the autonomous Grand Duchy under Russia preceded independence.

entries.title: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
entries.location: Central and eastern Europe · changing multiethnic territories
entries.note: The Union of Lublin joined the Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania in a common political framework. Earlier unions preceded 1569. The partitions ended the Commonwealth in 1795; its diverse populations and their histories continued.

entries.title: Poland · restored state and modern eras
entries.note: 1918 marks restoration after the partitions, not the beginning of Polish history. Nazi German and Soviet invasion and occupation from 1939, a government in exile, postwar border changes, communist government and the transition after 1989 interrupt any simple story of continuous sovereign rule.

entries.title: Kingdom of Hungary · changing royal realms
entries.note: Stephen’s coronation is conventionally dated 1000 or 1001. This umbrella covers major territorial division after 1526, Ottoman rule in central areas, Habsburg royal government and the 1867 dual monarchy; it is not one unchanged or continuously independent territory. Later restoration of the kingdom in 1920–1946 is outside this selected frame.

entries.title: Hungary · post-Habsburg and modern eras
entries.note: The Habsburg monarchy’s collapse in 1918 begins this selected modern frame. Republics, the 1920–1946 kingdom, wartime occupation, communist rule and the democratic transition after 1989 are distinct phases. Hungarian history and communities predate 1918 and extend beyond modern borders.

entries.title: Ireland · later medieval societies
entries.note: Uses the National Museum’s later-medieval convention, from church reform to the Reformation. Gaelic lordships, Anglo-Norman settlements, towns, religious communities and changing English claims overlapped. This is not a single unified Irish state, nor does 1550 mark the end of Gaelic culture.

entries.title: Dutch Republic · United Provinces
entries.note: 1588 conventionally marks the republican form after earlier revolt, the Union of Utrecht in 1579 and the Act of Abjuration in 1581. Recognition of independence followed in 1648. French invasion and the Batavian Revolution ended this republic in 1795; the modern kingdom began later.

entries.title: Netherlands · kingdom and modern state
entries.location: Northwestern Europe and the Kingdom’s Caribbean territories
entries.note: The kingdom proclaimed in 1815 initially included the southern provinces; Belgium separated in 1830 and was recognised in 1839. The present Kingdom comprises the Netherlands, Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. It is not identical to the earlier Dutch Republic or an unchanged colonial empire.

entries.title: Medieval Bulgarian states · first and second empires
entries.location: Balkans · shifting territories around present-day Bulgaria
entries.note: Groups the First Bulgarian Empire (681–1018) and Second (1185/1186–late fourteenth century), separated by Byzantine rule. 1396 is a conventional endpoint for Ottoman conquest; regional remnants and claims complicate an exact final date. It is not one uninterrupted empire.

entries.title: Bulgaria · principality, kingdom and republic
entries.note: The autonomous principality established in 1878 remained formally under Ottoman suzerainty until independence in 1908. The monarchy, communist republic and post-1989 parliamentary republic are separate phases; 1878 is not an origin date for Bulgarian people.

entries.title: Medieval Serbian realms
entries.dates: 1217–1459 CE · selected royal and successor phases
entries.note: 1217 marks Stefan’s royal coronation, after earlier Serbian principalities. Kingdom, empire and successor despotate are grouped here; their borders and degree of control changed. The Ottoman capture of Smederevo in 1459 ends this selected frame, not Serbian society.
entries.wikiTitle: History of Serbia in the Middle Ages

entries.title: Serbia · independent republic after state union
entries.note: 2006 marks the end of the state union with Montenegro, not the first Serbian state or independence. Serbia continued the union’s UN membership. Kosovo declared independence in 2008; its international status remains contested, and this listing does not resolve that dispute.

entries.title: Medieval Kingdom of Croatia · selected phase
entries.location: Eastern Adriatic and neighbouring inland regions
entries.note: 925 is the traditional royal convention associated with Tomislav; 1102 conventionally marks rule under the Hungarian crown. Details of the union and the later Pacta conventa text require caution. The range does not imply Croatia or Croatian institutions disappeared in 1102.

entries.title: Croatia · independent republic
entries.location: Croatia · eastern Adriatic and southeastern Europe
entries.note: 1991 dates declarations and implementation of independence from Yugoslavia, followed by war and later international recognition. Croatia joined the UN in 1992. This is a modern state convention, not the beginning of Croatian communities or institutions.

entries.title: Medieval Bosnia · bans and kings
entries.location: Bosnia and neighbouring western Balkan territories
entries.note: A rounded frame following the National Museum’s mid-tenth-century emergence of the medieval Bosnian state through changing bans and royal rule. The Ottoman conquest in 1463 ends this selected state frame; local communities, religious traditions and regional institutions continued.
entries.wikiTitle: History of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Middle Ages

entries.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina · independent state
entries.note: Independence and international recognition came in 1992 during Yugoslavia’s dissolution. War followed; the Dayton agreement in 1995 established the present constitutional framework. Bosnia and Herzegovina is one sovereign state with internal entities, not two independent countries.

entries.title: Yugoslav states · monarchy and changing federations
entries.note: The 1918 kingdom, wartime occupation and resistance, socialist federation, and 1992–2003 Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were different arrangements. The last became Serbia and Montenegro in 2003 and ended in 2006. The 1992 federation was not automatically accepted as the sole continuation of socialist Yugoslavia.

entries.title: Slovenia · independent republic
entries.note: The assembly adopted independence acts on 25 June 1991, followed by declaration and a short war. UN admission followed in 1992. This dates the selected sovereign state, not the origins of Slovene communities or the entire history of the territory.

entries.title: Montenegro · restored independence
entries.note: The referendum of 21 May was followed by parliament’s declaration on 3 June 2006, ending union with Serbia. Earlier Montenegrin statehood preceded Yugoslavia, so 2006 is restoration in a new constitutional setting rather than the beginning of Montenegrin history.

entries.title: North Macedonia · independent state
entries.note: The September 1991 referendum begins this selected independence frame. The state entered the UN in 1993 under a provisional designation; the country’s name changed to North Macedonia in 2019 after the Prespa agreement. Modern statehood is not a claim that one ancient polity survived unchanged.
